```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```


# Set working directory
# Tells R where to look for your files on your computer. It sets the active directory to your specified folder path so R can easily locate your Excel dataset.
```{r}
setwd("D:/CANON/Intermediate R")
```


# Load libraries
# Loads specialized packages required for the workflow: 
# cluster provides core clustering functions, factoextra helps visualize cluster outputs and optimal cluster metrics, and readxl allows R to read Excel spreadsheets directly.
```{r}
library(cluster)
library(dplyr)
library(factoextra)
library(readxl)
```


# Load the dataset 
```{r}
df <- read_excel("mall_customers.xlsx")
head(df)
```


# The structure of the dataset
```{r}
str(df)
```


# Select the numeric features for clustering (exclude Customer_ID)
```{r}
features <- df[, c("Age", "Annual_Income", "Spending_Score", 
                   "Years_As_Member", "Average_Purchase_Value")]
```



# Scale the data (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1)
# Standardizes the data so that every feature has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. 
# This step is vital because features with larger numerical ranges (like Annual Income or Average Purchase Value) would otherwise overpower smaller-scale features (like Years As Member).
```{r}
scaled_features <- scale(features)
```


# Determine the optimal number of clusters using the Elbow Method
# Calculates the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (wss) for various values of k. When plotted, it helps you identify the "elbow point"—the optimal number of clusters where adding more clusters yields diminishing returns.
```{r}
fviz_nbclust(scaled_features, kmeans, method = "wss") +
  labs(title = "Elbow Method for Optimal k (Multi-Feature Data)")
```


# Apply K-Means clustering (setting k = 3 based on typical cluster patterns)
# Runs the core machine learning algorithm. set.seed(42) ensures random initial centroid placements are reproducible so you get the exact same results every time you run it. centers = 3 tells the model to partition data into 3 groups, and nstart = 25 runs the algorithm 25 times with different starting configurations, picking the best local optimum.
```{r}
set.seed(42) # Ensures reproducibility
k_optimal <- 3
kmeans_result <- kmeans(scaled_features, centers = k_optimal, nstart = 25)
```


# View the cluster sizes and centers
```{r}
print(kmeans_result)
```


# Append the cluster assignments back to the original dataframe
```{r}
df$Cluster <- as.factor(kmeans_result$cluster)
head(df)
```


# Visualize the clusters using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduction
# Since we have 5 dimensions, PCA reduces them to 2D for plotting purposes
```{r}
fviz_cluster(kmeans_result, data = scaled_features,
             palette = c("#2E9FDF", "#00AFBB", "#E7B800"),
             geom = "point",
             ellipse.type = "convex",
             ggtheme = theme_minimal(),
             main = "Customer Clusters (5-Feature Model Visualized via PCA)"
)

```


# Because your data has 5 dimensions, it cannot be drawn directly on a standard 2D scatter plot. This function uses Principal Component Analysis (PCA) behind the scenes to compress the 5 features down into 2 principal components, plotting your customer groups with colored convex hulls and cluster points.
